match.reason: The closest bank point, Writing a historical explanation, is a Year 8 paragraph structure that does not teach dealing with other views or full source citation, which the Year 9 and 10 argument point requires, so a new point is needed.

draft.title: Writing a historical argument
card: A contention is the main claim of your argument. It answers the question with a clear position, such as "The gold rushes changed Victoria more than any other event of the 1850s".
Each point in your argument needs evidence from sources, such as a quote, a statistic or a described event. Explain how the evidence supports your claim.
A strong argument deals with other views. It admits a different view exists, then explains why the evidence supports your contention more.
Cite your sources so a reader can find them and check your evidence. Give the author or creator, the title and the date.
draft.remember: State a clear claim, back it with sourced evidence, answer other views and cite your sources.

a.q: Which sentence is a clear contention for an essay on why Federation happened in 1901?
opts: Fear of foreign powers and trade drove Federation
Many historians have written about Federation
The colonies had different tariffs and railway gauges
a.why: A contention takes a position that can be argued and supported with evidence. The statement that Federation happened in 1901 is a fact that nobody disputes, so it gives the essay nothing to argue.
a.clue: Which one takes a position that needs evidence to support it?

b.q: Tariq argues that railways did more than gold to grow Victoria's economy. A classmate says gold mattered most. What should Tariq do to deal with this other view in his essay?
opts: Explain why his evidence favours railways over gold
Leave out the gold view so his essay stays focused
Change his contention to say that gold mattered most
Add more quotes that agree with him and say nothing of gold
b.why: Dealing with other views means naming them and showing why the evidence favours your own claim. Ignoring the gold view leaves the argument open to challenge, even though it keeps the essay shorter.
b.clue: A strong argument faces the other view instead of avoiding it.

a.best: Fear of foreign powers and trade drove Federation

b.best: Explain why his evidence favours railways over gold
